text: Acacia drummondii, commonly known as Drummond's wattle, is a flowering plant in the family Fabaceae and is endemic to the south-west of Western Australia. It is a shrub that typically grows to a height of 0.3–2 m (1 ft 0 in – 6 ft 7 in), with bipinnate leaves on a petiole 0.5–5 mm (0.020–0.197 in) long, having up to four pairs of pinnae. The lower pinnae are 2–10 mm (0.079–0.394 in) long, while those near the end are 4–20 mm (0.16–0.79 in) long; each pinna has two or three lower pinnules and two to seven pinnules near the ends. The leaves are mid-green to slightly bluish green and can be smooth or densely hairy. The flowers are pale to golden yellow, arranged in single spikes 10–40 mm (0.39–1.57 in) long, borne in leaf axils on a peduncle 10–30 mm (0.39–1.18 in) long, with flowering occurring between June and October. The pods are narrowly oblong, rigid, dark or brownish-grey, measuring 15–50 mm (0.59–1.97 in) long and 3.5–8 mm (0.14–0.31 in) wide, and contain elliptic to oblong seeds 2–3.5 mm (0.079–0.138 in) wide. The species was first formally described in 1839 by botanist John Lindley in his book, A Sketch of the Vegetation of the Swan River Colony, with the specific epithet "drummondii" honoring James Drummond, the Government Naturalist of the Swan River Colony. Four subspecies of A. drummondii have been described and are accepted by the Australian Plant Census: subsp. candolleana, subsp. drummondii, subsp. elegans, and subsp. affinis. Drummond's wattle is found from near Mount Lesueur, south to Albany, and within the Fitzgerald River National Park, growing in granite outcrops, gullies, low-lying areas, and on hillsides in sandy and gravelly soils across the Avon Wheatbelt, Esperance Plains, Geraldton Sandplains, Jarrah Forest, Mallee, and Swan Coastal Plain bioregions of south-western Western Australia. Subspecies candolleana, drummondii, and elegans are classified as "not threatened," while subsp. affinis is listed as "Priority Three" by the Government of Western Australia Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, indicating it is poorly known, known from only a few locations, but not under imminent threat.
